title: Class 6 Maths Organising Data (Tally Marks, Pictographs & Bar Graphs) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 6 Maths Organising Data Explained + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Learn Class 6 maths organising data: tally marks, frequency tables, pictographs and bar graphs, with a solved case study and a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: A jumble of raw numbers tells you almost nothing until you organise it. Here is how the NCERT Class 6 data handling chapter turns a messy survey into tally marks, a frequency table and a readable bar graph — with a solved case study and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask thirty Class 6 students their favourite fruit and write the answers down as they shout them out, and what you get is a mess: mango, apple, mango, banana, orange, apple, mango… a page of scattered words that answers nothing. Which fruit won? You genuinely cannot tell by staring at the list. That single frustration is the whole point of the NCERT class 6 maths organising data chapter — raw information is nearly useless until you give it a shape. In my experience teaching eleven-year-olds, the moment they see a heap of jumbled answers turn into a neat table with a clear winner, the idea of data handling clicks for good.

This chapter (Data Handling in the NCERT textbook) is not about hard arithmetic. It is about four skills that build on each other: collecting raw data, organising it with tally marks into a frequency table, then showing it as a pictograph or a bar graph, and finally reading answers back out of those pictures. Get the order right and the rest is easy.

What ‘organising data’ actually means

Data is just a collection of numbers or facts gathered for a purpose — marks in a test, the number of siblings each child has, daily temperatures for a week. When you first collect it, it is raw data: unsorted, in the order it happened to arrive. Organising data means arranging that raw information so a pattern jumps out.

The simplest tool is a list sorted into groups. If eight children scored 7 out of 10 on a spelling test, you do not want ‘7’ written eight times in random spots on the page. You want one row that says: score 7, eight children. That row is the seed of a frequency table.

Tally marks and frequency tables

Tally marks are the fastest honest way to count as you go. You draw one vertical stroke for each item, and here is the rule students most often forget: the fifth stroke is drawn across the previous four, making a bundle of five. Counting in fives is far quicker and far less error-prone than counting a long row of single strokes.

The number you get for each category is its frequency — how many times that value occurred. Put the categories, their tally marks and their frequencies side by side and you have a frequency table. Here is one built from a survey of 30 students asked how many pets they keep at home.

Number of petsTally marksFrequency (no. of students)
0|||| ||||9
1|||| |||| ||12
2|||| |6
3|||3

Notice the check that catches most mistakes: the frequencies must add up to the total number of students. 9 + 12 + 6 + 3 = 30. If your total does not match how many people you surveyed, you miscounted somewhere — go back before you draw anything.

Pictographs: pictures that count

A pictograph shows data using a symbol, where one symbol stands for a fixed number of items. A picture of one apple might stand for 5 apples sold. If a shop sold 20 apples on Monday, you draw four apples in Monday’s row.

The part students trip on is the key (also called the scale). Half a symbol means half the value — if one book picture means 10 books, then half a book means 5. Always read the key first. A pictograph without a key is just decoration; the key is what turns it into data.

When a pictograph works best

  • When the numbers are small, whole multiples of the symbol value.
  • When you want something friendly and visual for a younger audience or a poster.
  • When you are comparing a few categories at a glance, not doing precise arithmetic.

Bar graphs: the workhorse

A bar graph uses rectangular bars of equal width, with the height (or length) of each bar showing the frequency. The bars stand apart with equal gaps, and the scale on the vertical axis decides how tall each bar climbs. Choosing a sensible scale is the real skill — if the largest frequency is 12, a scale of 1 unit = 2 students keeps the graph a readable size, while 1 unit = 1 student may run off the page.

Bar graphs beat pictographs when numbers are larger or awkward, because you are not forced to draw half and quarter symbols. To read a bar graph, run your eye from the top of a bar across to the scale — that value is the frequency for that category.

A solved case study: the canteen survey

Here is the kind of real-life passage that appears in exams, close to the ones in our case-study book. Read it, then work the questions.

The Class 6 monitor surveyed all 40 students about their favourite canteen snack. The results were: Samosa 14, Sandwich 6, Pasta 8, Vada Pav 12. She drew a bar graph with a scale of 1 unit = 2 students.

  • Q1. Which snack was most popular? Samosa, with a frequency of 14 — the tallest bar.
  • Q2. How many units tall is the Vada Pav bar? 12 students ÷ 2 per unit = 6 units.
  • Q3. How many more students chose Samosa than Sandwich? 14 − 6 = 8 students.
  • Q4. Do the frequencies confirm the survey size? 14 + 6 + 8 + 12 = 40, which matches the class strength, so nobody was missed.

That last check — adding the frequencies back to the total — is worth a mark on its own and takes five seconds. Teach students to do it every single time.

The mistakes I see most often

Three errors account for almost every lost mark in this chapter. First, forgetting to write or read the key on a pictograph, so a symbol worth 10 gets counted as 1. Second, drawing bars of unequal width or with uneven gaps, which makes the graph lie about the data. Third, misreading the scale on a bar graph — counting gridlines instead of the values they represent. None of these are about being bad at maths; they are about slowing down for two seconds and reading the labels.

Try the quiz, then the case studies

Below is a free 8-question quiz on exactly this chapter — tally marks, frequency, reading pictographs and bar graphs. Let your child try it, then go through the explanations for anything they miss. quiz.title: Class 6 Organising Data Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on tally marks, frequency tables, pictographs and bar graphs. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 6 data handling and organising data

questions.q: In tally marks, how do you show the number 5?
options: Four strokes with a fifth crossing them
questions.explanation: Every fifth tally is drawn across the previous four to make a bundle of five, which makes counting faster.

questions.q: What is the frequency of a value in a data set?
questions.explanation: Frequency is simply the number of times a particular value or category appears in the data.

questions.q: A frequency table shows 8, 12, 6 and 4 students for four scores. How many were surveyed?
questions.explanation: Add the frequencies: 8 + 12 + 6 + 4 = 30 students in total.

questions.q: In a pictograph, one book symbol stands for 10 books. What does half a book symbol mean?
questions.explanation: Half a symbol means half its value, so half of 10 is 5 books.

questions.q: Which is the main reason to use tally marks while collecting data?
options: They count quickly in groups of five
They are the same as a bar graph
questions.explanation: Tally marks let you count as data arrives, and the bundles of five make totalling quick and accurate.

questions.q: In a bar graph, what does the height of a bar represent?
questions.explanation: The height (or length) of each bar shows the frequency of the category it stands for.

questions.q: A bar graph uses a scale of 1 unit = 2 students. A bar 5 units tall represents how many students?
questions.explanation: Multiply the units by the scale: 5 units times 2 students per unit = 10 students.

questions.q: A survey of 25 students records 10, 7 and 6 for three snacks, but the graph shows a fourth snack. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation: The frequencies must total 25, so the fourth is 25 minus (10 + 7 + 6) = 25 minus 23 = 2 students.

faq.q: What is the difference between raw data and organised data?
faq.a: Raw data is information written down in the order it was collected, unsorted — like a list of shouted-out answers. Organised data is that same information arranged into groups, tally marks or a table so a pattern is easy to see.

faq.q: Why is the fifth tally mark drawn across the other four?
faq.a: Crossing every fifth stroke bundles the marks into fives, so you count 5, 10, 15 instead of counting single strokes one by one. It is faster and you make far fewer counting errors on large data sets.

faq.q: When should I use a bar graph instead of a pictograph?
faq.a: Use a bar graph when the numbers are large or awkward, because you would otherwise have to draw fractions of a symbol. Pictographs suit small, tidy numbers and a friendly, visual look; bar graphs are the workhorse for exam data.

faq.q: How do I read a value from a bar graph correctly?
faq.a: Look at the top of the bar, then move straight across to the vertical scale and read the value there — remembering the scale, so if 1 unit means 2 students a bar of 6 units is 12 students. Count the scale values, not the gridlines.
